explanations.explanation: Yes, friend, the Jordan. Joshua and all the Israelites leave Shittim and go as far as the Jordan, where they camp before crossing over (Joshua 3:1). Notice the "before crossing over" part. Nobody is moving in yet, they're just parking at the edge of a very big river.

The Jabbok is a real river, friend, but it's not the one in this passage. The text says they went as far as the Jordan, where they camped before crossing over (Joshua 3:1). Easy one to mix up, since rivers all look alike when you're hauling a whole camp.
The Arnon is another river, but Joshua 3:1 says they went as far as the Jordan. That's where they camped before crossing over. I mix up my own spice jars all the time, so no shame here.

explanations.answer: Set out from their spots and follow it
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The officers tell the people, "When you see the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God being carried by the Levitical priests, you are to set out from your positions and follow it." (Joshua 3:3). The signal is simple. See the ark moving, then you move.

explanations.answer: Bow down and stay in their tents
explanations.explanation: Close to a lot of things people do around holy items, but not here. The officers say to set out from their positions and follow the ark (Joshua 3:3). Staying in the tents would have meant a very quiet, very stuck camp.

explanations.answer: Gather around it and wait for Joshua
explanations.explanation: Nope, no waiting around in a huddle. The command is that when they see the ark carried by the Levitical priests, they set out from their positions and follow it (Joshua 3:3). The text doesn't have them gathering around it at all.

explanations.answer: So they can see the way to go
explanations.explanation: Right on, friend. The officers say to keep that distance "so that you can see the way to go, since you have never traveled this way before." (Joshua 3:4). Think of trying to read a map with someone's shoulder in your face. Space helps you see.

explanations.answer: So the camp stays out of sight
explanations.explanation: Hiding isn't the reason given. The text says the gap is "so that you can see the way to go, since you have never traveled this way before." (Joshua 3:4). Nothing in the passage says anyone is trying to stay out of sight.

explanations.answer: So the priests can walk faster
explanations.explanation: I like the thinking, but the text gives a different reason. The gap is so the people can see the way to go, since they have never traveled this way before (Joshua 3:4). Nobody is racing here, baker.

explanations.answer: Tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among them
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Joshua says, "Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you." (Joshua 3:5). The reason points straight at what the LORD is about to do. I'd have cleaned my whole apron for that news.

explanations.answer: Tomorrow the priests will offer sacrifices
explanations.explanation: Sacrifices are a real thing in Scripture, but they're not Joshua's reason here. He says to consecrate themselves because "tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you." (Joshua 3:5). The focus is on what the LORD will do.

explanations.answer: Tomorrow the kings of Canaan will attack
explanations.explanation: An attack would sure get my attention, friend, but Joshua doesn't say that. His reason is that "tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you." (Joshua 3:5). It's a promise of wonders, not a warning of a battle.

Yes, Moses, Israel's leader before Joshua. The LORD says He will exalt Joshua so all Israel may know He is with him "just as I was with Moses." (Joshua 3:7). That's a big thing to hear about a new leader. Joshua has some big sandals to fill, and God says He'll be with him in them.

Aaron, Moses' brother and Israel's first high priest (Exodus 28:1), is a good name to know, but he isn't the one here. The LORD says He is with Joshua "just as I was with Moses." (Joshua 3:7). Easy to get tangled up when those two walked together so much.

Abraham, the father of Israel's people (Genesis 12:1-2), is a great name, but not the one in this line. The LORD says He will be with Joshua "just as I was with Moses." (Joshua 3:7). Moses led the people out, and now Joshua is leading them in.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says the opposite: "When you reach the edge of the waters, stand in the Jordan." (Joshua 3:8). The priests don't stay on the bank. They walk right in, and that's a lot of trust.
That's right, baker. The LORD tells Joshua to command the priests, "When you reach the edge of the waters, stand in the Jordan." (Joshua 3:8). No staying on the bank with dry toes. They go in.
Not this time, friend. Joshua says, "Now choose twelve men from the tribes of Israel, one from each tribe." (Joshua 3:12). That's twelve men from twelve tribes, not twelve from Levi.

You've got it, baker. Joshua says to choose twelve men from the tribes of Israel, "one from each tribe." (Joshua 3:12). So it's one man per tribe, not a whole dozen from Levi. Fair is fair, even in my cookie boxes.

explanations.answer: Stop and stand up in a heap
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Joshua says that when the priests' feet touch down in the Jordan, "its flowing waters will be cut off and will stand up in a heap." (Joshua 3:13). Water standing up in a heap. I can't even get my frosting to do that.

explanations.answer: Rise up and flood the camp
explanations.explanation: A flood would've been a scary day, friend, but that's not the promise. Joshua says the flowing waters "will be cut off and will stand up in a heap." (Joshua 3:13). The water is cut off, not coming for the camp.

explanations.answer: Drop down to a shallow stream
explanations.explanation: A shallow stream would be a gentle surprise, but Joshua says something bigger. The flowing waters "will be cut off and will stand up in a heap." (Joshua 3:13). Cut off and heaped up, not just thinned out.
Not quite, friend. The text says, "the Jordan overflows its banks throughout the harvest season." (Joshua 3:15). So at harvest time it's running high, not low.
Right, baker. Joshua 3:15 says the Jordan overflows its banks throughout the harvest season. That's high water, not low. It makes the priests walking up to it that much bolder.

That's right, friend. Once the water is cut off, "the people crossed over opposite Jericho." (Joshua 3:16). The river stops and the people walk across right in front of Jericho. That's a view the city could not miss.

It's actually true, friend. Joshua 3:16 says the water was cut off, "So the people crossed over opposite Jericho." The crossing happens right across from the city. Good thing you can always flip it back and try again next time.
Yes, dry. The priests carrying the ark "stood firm on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan" (Joshua 3:17). Dry ground in the middle of a river. I'd tell that story at every party.

That's right, baker. The priests stood firm while all Israel crossed over "until the entire nation had crossed the Jordan." (Joshua 3:17). Every last person made it across, and the priests held their spot the whole time.

Muddy would've made for a messy walk, friend, but the text says the priests stood firm on dry ground (Joshua 3:17). Dry ground, with the whole nation crossing over it. My boots would have said thank you.

A council sounds official, but it's not the word here. The priests stand firm until "the entire nation had crossed the Jordan." (Joshua 3:17). The whole nation crossed, not just a few leaders in a meeting.

The priests are the ones standing in the river, so I see why this one tempts you. But the text says they stood firm "until the entire nation had crossed the Jordan." (Joshua 3:17). They're holding the ark while everybody else goes across.
